content: Boutonneuse fever, also known as Kenya tick typhus, Marseille fever, Mediterranean spotted fever, or fièvre boutonneuse, is a febrile illness caused by a Rickettsial infection. The causative agent is the bacterium Rickettsia conorii, which is transmitted to humans through the bite of the dog tick, Rhipicephalus sanguineus. This disease is endemic in many countries surrounding the Mediterranean Sea. The incubation period for Boutonneuse fever is approximately 7 days. Clinical symptoms include fever, joint pain, chills, headache, muscle aches (myalgias), and sensitivity to light (photophobia). On physical examination, a characteristic black eschar, known as tache noire, may be observed at the site of the tick bite. Around the fourth day of illness, a skin rash (exanthem) typically develops. This rash initially appears as macular (flat, discolored spots) and may progress to maculopapular (raised, discolored spots) or even petechial (small red or purple spots caused by bleeding under the skin). The diagnosis of Boutonneuse fever is confirmed through serologic testing. Traditional methods include the Weil-Felix test, which detects agglutination of Proteus OX strains. More modern diagnostic techniques involve enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunofluorescence assays. The cornerstone of treatment for Boutonneuse fever is antimicrobial therapy. For adults, the preferred regimen is doxycycline, administered as 200 mg orally twice daily for 1 day, or alternatively, 200 mg or 100 mg orally twice daily for 2 to 5 days. If doxycycline is contraindicated, alternative regimens include josamycin (1 g every 8 hours for 7 days) or ciprofloxacin.
